figure_inventory.caption: The learning sequence used in every chapter.
A dependency view of the book. Foundations and the harness come first; the other parts branch from there.
SKETCH The big picture for this chapter: the model is a narrow, powerful text predictor; everything around it — memory, actions, validation, retries — is the runtime's job.

How generation works: for the prompt "Your refund will be processed within…", the model assigns a probability to every possible next token. Low temperature concentrates choices on the top candidate; high temperature spreads them out (illustrative).
The anatomy of a single model call. Everything left of the model is assembled by your application; everything right of it must be parsed and validated by your application.
The structured-output safety net: constrain the format, validate the meaning, repair a bounded number of times, then fail loudly.
The tool-calling round trip. The model proposes; the runtime validates, authorises, executes and reports back.
flags: Typography screening: non-header page text below approximately6pt; check figure-label legibility.

figure_inventory.caption: Illustrative latency model for one call (TTFT 0.6 s, 60 output tokens/s). Output length, not input length, usually dominates — which is why concise structured decisions make agents faster.
The model is a pure function; the runtime owns every form of state. Swapping the model must not lose anything the system knows.
X-RAY X-ray of one chat reply. Six words from the user became a 3,412-token request; the reply came back token by token, with usage and a stop reason the runtime must check.
A provider-neutral model interface. Agent code depends only on the interface; adapters translate to each vendor's API.
SKETCH The big picture: an agent is a loop in which a model chooses the next action, wrapped in deterministic controls that decide what is allowed and when to stop.
Who decides the next step? Moving right gives more flexibility — and more variance, cost and risk to bound.
Framework-independent agent anatomy. The model is one component among many; most of the box is ordinary, deterministic software.
EXPLODED VIEW Exploded view of an agent. Only one of the seven parts is probabilistic; the other six are authored, deterministic and testable.
The agent loop. Each iteration is bounded by checks the controller performs before and after the model decides.
The deterministic sandwich: code before and after the single probabilistic step.
Autonomy levels. Most enterprise agents operate at different levels for different actions — fully autonomous for reads, supervised for writes.
What a run budget does: cumulative cost of a looping run with and without a hard cap (illustrative).
SKETCH The big picture: every control pattern answers "who decides the next step, and when?"
The main control patterns, arranged from most deterministic (left) to most model- directed (right).
ReAct in action: each observation changes what the model does next.
flags: Typography screening: non-header page text below approximately6pt; check figure-label legibility.

figure_inventory.caption: X-RAY X-ray of a ReAct run. Two useful turns, one repeated search with identical arguments, and a loop guard that turned the stall into an answer.
A router classifies once, then hands off to a specialised, cheaper or safer handler.
The hybrid shape used in many production agents: a short, reviewable plan whose steps are each executed by a small bounded ReAct loop.
Plan-and-execute with replanning. Replans are triggered by failures or evidence that invalidates later steps — and are themselves budgeted.
Illustrative comparison for a 4-step support task: model calls and p50 latency. ReAct adapts but spends a call per step; plan-and-execute front-loads one larger call; reflection roughly doubles cost.
SKETCH The big picture: instructions are layered, composed from versioned packs, and released like code — while untrusted content stays data.
The instruction hierarchy. Authority flows from top to bottom; content lower down may inform the agent but must never override what is above it.
EXPLODED VIEW Exploded view of a production system prompt. Seven plates, sized by tokens; together they form the stable, cacheable prefix of every call.
flags: Figure 4.3: exploded plates have isolated token units; inspect missing numeric labels.

figure_inventory.caption: Composing a system prompt from versioned instruction packs. Each pack has an owner and tests; the composed prompt is recorded with every run.
The prompt release pipeline. A prompt version moves through the same gates as application code, and every run records the version it used.
SKETCH The big picture: the harness wraps the model in components that decide what it sees, what it may do, what is recorded and when it stops.
Harness components. Every arrow crossing into the model or out to tools passes through a component that can validate, authorise, record or refuse.
Run lifecycle states. Transitions are controlled by the harness, never directly by model output.
flags: Typography screening: non-header page text below approximately6pt; check figure-label legibility.

figure_inventory.caption: One harness step. The model is consulted once; every other interaction is mediated by harness components.
flags: Typography screening: non-header page text below approximately6pt; check figure-label legibility.

figure_inventory.caption: Where each concern lives. One owner per concern prevents duplicated retries, skipped checks and inconsistent limits.
X-RAY X-ray of one turn. The user sees a confirmation; underneath, the harness built the context, checked policy, executed with an idempotency key, recorded state and checked the output.
SKETCH The big picture: a tool call travels through a fixed series of checkpoints before anything real happens.
The two faces of a tool. The model only ever sees the contract; the runtime wraps the implementation in controls the model cannot bypass.
EXPLODED VIEW Exploded view of a tool. The model-facing contract is three plates; the runtime wrapper the model cannot bypass is four more.
Choosing a retry policy for a tool call. The tool's side-effect class and idempotency, not the model, decide.
Why idempotency keys matter. The retry carries the same key, so the payment service returns the original result instead of refunding twice.
flags: Typography screening: non-header page text below approximately6pt; check figure-label legibility.

figure_inventory.caption: Trust boundaries around tools. Outputs from tools that touch external or user- generated content are untrusted and labelled as such before entering context.
SKETCH The big picture: events are the source of truth, reducers fold them into state, checkpoints snapshot it, and context is only a temporary view.
Context is a view built from state and memory for one model call. State is the source of truth; context is disposable.
EXPLODED VIEW Exploded view of a run state. Seven parts, each answering a question a new worker or an investigator would ask before continuing the run.
Event sourcing in one picture: state at any step is the fold of all events up to that step — so you can inspect the run at step 5 as easily as at the end (illustrative budget usage).
Event-sourced state. Components emit events; reducers fold them into state; snapshots (checkpoints) avoid replaying the whole history.
Crash and resume. Because the intent and idempotency key were checkpointed before the mutation, the resumed worker completes it exactly once.

figure_inventory.caption: SKETCH The big picture: many sources compete for a small window; policy filters, ranking and budgets decide what the model actually sees.
The context builder. Sources are filtered by policy, ranked by priority, fitted into per- section budgets and assembled into a stable order.
